prompt:
A student needs to estimate the thickness of a single sheet of standard photocopier paper.
(a) Explain why directly measuring the thickness of a single sheet with a standard $30\text{ cm}$ plastic ruler is impossible. [1]
(b) Describe a practical laboratory procedure to obtain a reliable estimate of the thickness using a stack of 500 identical sheets and the $30\text{ cm}$ ruler. [2]
(c) The height of the 500-sheet stack is measured as $5.0\text{ cm}$. Calculate the estimated thickness of one sheet in millimetres ($\text{mm}$). [1]
answer:
(a) The thickness of one sheet (~0.1 mm) is much smaller than the smallest division (1 mm) on the ruler.
(b) Measure the total height of the 500-sheet ream with the ruler, then divide the total measured height by 500.
(c) 0.10 mm

mark_scheme.criterion: (a) States that a single sheet thickness is much smaller than the resolution / smallest division (1 mm) of the ruler.
(b) States measuring the total height / thickness of the 500-sheet stack.
(b) States dividing the total measured height by 500.
(c) 0.10 mm (or 0.1 mm / 1.0 x 10^-4 m); both value and unit required.

hints: What is the smallest division on a school ruler (1 mm)?
How can you multiply the small thickness to make it readable on the ruler?
solution:
(a) A single sheet of paper has a thickness of approximately 0.1 mm, which is ten times smaller than the 1 mm smallest division of the ruler. It cannot be resolved individually.
(b) Procedure:
1. Place the complete ream of 500 sheets on a flat surface and measure the total stack height using the ruler.
2. Divide the total measured height by 500 to obtain the average thickness of a single sheet.
(c) Stack height = 5.0 cm = 50 mm.
Thickness of one sheet = 50 mm / 500 = 0.10 mm (or 1.0 x 10^-4 m).
teacher_walkthrough: Core Cambridge practical technique: amplifying small dimensions through multiple samples.
Emphasize unit conversion: converting 5.0 cm to 50 mm before dividing by 500 avoids decimal errors.
